extracted.intended_audience: general public, students, policymakers, and health policy researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and interpret statutory, constitutional, and procedural rules and program eligibility requirements appearing in the Affordable Care Act (ACA) coverage, implementation, and expansion debate. Useful for readers assessing how the law was enacted and how implementation options and constraints affect coverage outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origination requirement for revenue bills (House)
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States Constitution requires all revenue-related bills to originate in the House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To formally comply with this requirement the Senate repurposed H.R. 3590 (an unrelated House-passed revenue bill) as the vehicle for its healthcare reform proposal, discarding the bill's original content. This demonstrates a commonly used legislative tactic: using a House-originated bill as a procedural vehicle in the Senate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconciliation procedure limits and filibuster immunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Per the Congressional Budget Act of 1974, reconciliation cannot be subject to a filibuster. But reconciliation is limited to budget changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reconciliation cannot be filibustered, House Democrats used it to pass the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act for budgetary changes (e.g., higher subsidy levels, different taxes, removing the Nebraska Medicaid deal). However, non-budgetary regulations cannot be enacted via reconciliation, limiting what may be changed through that process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate cloture threshold to end debate (60 votes)
rubrics_metrics.description: With a Republican Senate minority vowing to filibuster, 60 votes would be necessary to pass the Senate; cloture votes require 60 votes to end debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Senate reached a 60–39 cloture vote on December 23 to end debate on the bill. The requirement for 60 votes to overcome filibuster shaped negotiation strategy (e.g., appealing to centrists and independents) and motivated use of reconciliation for some changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court (2012) constraint on Medicaid coercion (state option)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court ruling in 2012 held that states would not lose Medicaid funding if they did not expand Medicaid under the ACA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This decision effectively made the Medicaid expansion optional for states; several states rejected the expansion as a result. The ruling constrained federal ability to coerce states via threat of lost funding and altered the national coverage impact of the ACA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medicaid expansion statutory eligibility baseline (133% FPL reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory Medicaid expansion was framed around an income threshold of approximately 133% of the federal poverty line (FPL).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice many states set eligibility thresholds significantly below 133% FPL prior to expansion; states that adopted the expansion extended eligibility toward that benchmark. The 133% FPL level also interacts with exchange subsidy rules (see below).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exchange subsidies not available to individuals below the poverty line
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsidies on exchange insurance plans were not available to those below the poverty line, leaving some low-income adults without new coverage options if their state did not expand Medicaid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in Kansas non-disabled adults without children with incomes from 32% to 100% of the poverty line were ineligible both for Medicaid (state rules) and for exchange subsidies, creating a coverage gap. Studies estimated millions fell into this gap when states declined expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 1115 waivers for state-specific implementations (private option, work requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: States can use Section 1115 waivers to implement alternative Medicaid expansion designs (e.g., Arkansas's 'private option') and to add features like work requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arkansas implemented expansion through a Section 1115 waiver and later added a work requirement (added 2018, removed 2021). Use of waivers allows states to seek federal approval for nonstandard approaches to expansion but may lead to variation in coverage and rules across states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyde Amendment principles applied to exchanges / Executive Order 13535
rubrics_metrics.description: Compromise language and Executive Order 13535 were used to reaffirm Hyde Amendment principles, modifying the bill to give states the right to prohibit coverage of abortion within their own insurance exchanges and to continue banning the use of federal funds for abortion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, this meant that if a state prohibited abortion coverage in its exchange, consumers in that state would have to pay out of pocket for abortion services. The Executive Order was used as a political and procedural tool to secure support from pro-life members of Congress whose concerns could not be addressed in a reconciliation bill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of ACA excise taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: The ACA imposed excise taxes that raised revenue—for example, $11.3 billion from an excise tax on health insurers based on market share and $3 billion annually from taxes on importers and manufacturers of prescription drugs (total $16.3 billion in fiscal year 2015).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These taxes were part of the law's financing package; some provisions (e.g., the 'Cadillac' tax) were later repealed or modified. The placement and targets of excise taxes affected stakeholders differently (insurers, drug makers, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual mandate tax penalty specification and later zeroing
rubrics_metrics.description: The individual mandate penalty was specified as $695 per individual or $2,085 per family at a minimum, up to 2.5% of household income (whichever was higher); the tax penalty was set to $0 beginning in 2019 by later legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mandate penalty produced federal revenues (in fiscal year 2018, individual and employer mandates yielded $4 billion each) and was intended to enforce broad participation; zeroing the penalty changed incentives and affected coverage estimates.
